content: Lysosomal-associated membrane protein 1 (LAMP-1), also referred to as lysosome-associated membrane glycoprotein 1 or CD107a (Cluster of Differentiation 107a), is a protein encoded by the LAMP1 gene in humans. The LAMP1 gene is located on chromosome 13, specifically on the long arm (q) at region 3, band 4 (13q34). LAMP-1 belongs to a family of lysosome-associated membrane glycoproteins and is classified as a type I transmembrane glycoprotein. It is expressed at medium to high levels in at least 76 different types of normal tissue cells. LAMP-1 is predominantly localized to lysosomal membranes, where it provides carbohydrate ligands for selectins. Additionally, CD107a is recognized as a marker of degranulation in lymphocytes, such as CD8+ T cells and natural killer (NK) cells, and it may also play a role in tumor cell differentiation and metastasis. Structure LAMP-1 glycoproteins are primarily located on lysosomal membranes. Structurally, they consist of a large, highly glycosylated extracellular domain with N-linked carbohydrate chains on the luminal side of the membrane, and a short C-terminal tail that is exposed to the cytoplasm. The extracytoplasmic region contains a hinge-like structure capable of forming disulfide bridges, which are homologous to those found in human immunoglobulin A. Key structural features of LAMP-1 include: A polypeptide core with a molecular weight of approximately 40 kDa. 18 N-glycosylation sites that facilitate the addition of sugar chains. Polylactosamine attachments that protect the glycoprotein from degradation by lysosomal proteases. High levels of polylactosaminoglycan and sialic acid, which allow the glycoprotein to traverse the trans-Golgi network. Poly-N-acetyllactosamine groups, which are involved in interactions with selectins and other glycan-binding proteins. Function LAMP-1 and LAMP-2 glycoproteins together constitute approximately 50% of all lysosomal membrane proteins. They are believed to play a role in maintaining lysosomal integrity, regulating pH, and facilitating catabolic processes. The expression of LAMP-1 and LAMP-2 is interrelated; a deficiency in LAMP1 gene expression leads to compensatory upregulation of LAMP2, suggesting overlapping functions in vivo. However, this interdependence complicates the determination of LAMP-1’s specific role. While LAMP-1 deficiency alone does not result in significant phenotypic changes due to LAMP-2 compensation, the simultaneous deficiency of both LAMP-1 and LAMP-2 results in embryonic lethality. Although LAMP-1 is primarily localized to lysosomal membranes, it can also be expressed on the plasma membrane under certain conditions. This occurs when lysosomes fuse with the cell membrane. On the cell surface, LAMP-1 can act as a ligand for selectins, facilitating cell-cell adhesion. Surface expression of LAMP-1 is observed in cells with migratory or invasive functions, such as cytotoxic T cells, platelets, and macrophages. Furthermore, LAMP-1 and LAMP-2 are frequently expressed on the surface of cancer cells, particularly those with high metastatic potential, such as colon carcinoma and melanoma. The surface expression of LAMP-1 in these cancer cells has been shown to correlate with their metastatic behavior. Role in Cancer LAMP-1 expression on the surface of tumor cells has been documented in various cancer types, particularly in highly metastatic cancers such as pancreatic cancer, colon cancer, and melanoma. The structural properties of LAMP-1 are associated with tumor cell differentiation and metastatic potential, as it is thought to mediate cell-cell adhesion and migration. The adhesion of certain cancer cells to the extracellular matrix is facilitated by interactions between LAMP-1, LAMP-2, E-selectin, and galectins, with LAMP-1 and LAMP-2 serving as ligands for these cell adhesion molecules. Surface expression of LAMP-1 has been observed in the following cancer types: Human fibrosarcoma, Colon adenocarcinoma, Melanoma, Pancreatic adenocarcinoma, and Astrocytoma.
